script.title: Why Trains Refilled Water Without Stopping

lines: A fireman lowered a scoop into water between the rails at full speed.
In 1860, a railway wanted to speed up the Irish mail train.
Engineer John Ramsbottom had to run it from Chester to Holyhead in 2 hours 5 minutes.
But engines usually stopped on the way to take in water.
An ordinary run used 1,800 to 1,900 gallons.
In stormy weather, it could rise to 2,400 gallons.
The largest tenders only held 2,000 gallons.
You see, it's like holding your hand out of a car window.
The faster you go, the harder it pushes.
A scoop moving through a trough forced water up a pipe into a tank.
At 15 miles an hour, the water reached the top of the delivery pipe.
The fireman had to watch the water level closely.
If he raised the scoop too late, water burst from the vents and soaked the tender and footplate.
The spray behind the scoop could drench passengers.
So guards warned the first coach to keep the windows closed.
Once, two trains passed at a trough.
The spray scattered lumps of coal and broke the other train's windows.
The railway changed the timetable so it could not happen again.

claims.claim: When a steam locomotive passes over the trough lying between the rails, a water scoop can be lowered by the fireman, and the speed of forward motion forces water into the scoop, up the scoop pipe and into the tanks.

In 1860 the London and North-Western Company decided to accelerate the Irish mail; Mr. Ramsbottom, their chief mechanical engineer, was asked to make the run between Chester and Holyhead in 2 hours 5 minutes; the usual stop on the road to take in water had to be avoided.
In an ordinary way 1,800 to 1,900 gallons were consumed; in rough and stormy weather along the coast of North Wales consumption rose to 2,400 gallons; the largest tenders only held 2,000 gallons.

Ramsbottom arranged experiments and showed that the forward motion of a scoop in a trough of water would force water up a connected pipe and into a tank; at 15 miles an hour the water was raised to the top of the delivery pipe.
The fireman had to observe the water level indicator carefully; failure to raise the scoop promptly expelled large volumes of water from the vents, soaking the tender and footplate.
Taking water at speed causes considerable spray behind the scoop that risks drenching passengers; in Great Britain the guard warned passengers in the first coach to keep the windows closed.

Two trains passed each other at a water trough; the other train suffered broken windows due to lumps of tender coal scattered by the spray, and management retimetabled the trains so this could not happen again.

cast.fireman: a 30 year old English railway fireman with a soot-blackened round face, heavy black eyebrows, short black hair under a flat cloth cap, a dark green wool jacket with brass buttons and a red neckerchief, 1860s
cast.ramsbottom: a 46 year old English railway engineer with a long narrow face, receding brown hair, a full brown beard, wire spectacles and a dark brown frock coat over a grey waistcoat, 1860s
cast.guard: a 52 year old British railway guard with a ruddy round face, big white mutton-chop whiskers, a black peaked cap and a dark blue frock coat with brass buttons, 1860s
cast.passenger: a 26 year old English woman with copper red hair in a bun under a small dark green bonnet, pale freckled skin, a dark green travelling dress with a white collar, 1860s
cast.manager: a 58 year old British railway manager with a gaunt pale face, a bald head with grey side hair, a long grey goatee, half-moon spectacles, a black frock coat and a grey cravat, 1860s
